Learning Objectives
Review the clinically relevant differences in development, anatomy, physiology, nutrition, and
bone health.
Identify musculoskeletal disorders and medical conditions that are more common in and
unique to female athletes.
Recognize epidemiological sex differences in musculoskeletal sports injuries, including
concussions, patellofemoral pain syndrome, anterior cruciate ligament injuries, shoulder
instability, femoroacetabular impingement, and stress injuries.
Explain injury prevention strategies unique to female athletes.
Identify at-risk female athletes for serious conditions, including abuse and relative energy
deficiency in sports, formerly referred to as the female athlete triad.

Growth and Development
Bone Mass Acquisition and Loss
Peak bone mass (PBM) refers to the maximum amount of bone accrued at the end of young
adulthood.1 PBM helps predict the risk for future fractures and the development of
osteoporosis because bone density decreases with aging.
Males and females demonstrate unique differences in bone diameter and cortical thickness.1
Males and females experience the greatest acquisition of bone mass during puberty, at which
time rapid bone growth occurs. During this period, specific differences are noted between
males and females in bone length and cortical thickness of bones. Specifically, females have an
increased cortical thickness and decreased endosteal diameter via endosteal bone formation
pathways that include inhibition of periosteal apposition2 (Figure 1).

Numerous factors influence adult PBM, including genetic factors (33% to 50%) and lifestyle
factors (20% to 40%).3
A paucity of data are available from randomized controlled trials, identifying key differences in
the manner in which exercise influences bone mass acquisition between males and females;
however, observational studies have demonstrated a higher bone mineral density (BMD) and
bone mineral content in children who are physically active compared to sedentary
counterparts.4 This is thought to occur via the principles of Wolff’s law, in which bone
remodeling occurs during periods of skeletal growth with increasing load strain across the
appendicular skeleton.
Sex hormones play a critical role in overall bone development. Low levels of androgens and
estrogens help initiate the pubertal growth spurt via insulin-like growth factor-1 and growth
hormone pathways5
In addition, sex hormones have different sex-specific effects on bone development. For
example, elevated pubescent estrogen levels in females results in endocortical apposition,
decreased periosteal bone expansion, and epiphyseal closure.1 Pubescent male estrogen
levels trigger periosteal expansion in addition to the trabecular bone formation associated
with male androgen levels.6 The multitude of complex cell-signal pathways initiated via sex
hormones helps shape the unique differences in bone structure between males and females.
Physiologic Differences in the Female Athlete
Numerous physiologic differences exist between female and male athletes7 (Table 1).
Females have a wider pelvic girdle, narrower shoulders, and a lower center of gravity than
males.
Females also have a higher percentage of body fat (18% to 20%) compared with males (10% to
15%), lower muscle mass per body weight, decreased bone mass, and decreased overall
aerobic capacity with a decreased VO2max and thoracic capacity.7,8

Nutrition Considerations
Caloric Requirements
Sports nutrition plays a key role in the overall health and well-being of all athletes.
Understanding caloric requirements is essential to reaching athletic goals and maintaining
good health. A sports nutritionist is a vital member of the sports medicine team. Athletes
should keep a diary, understand appropriate dietary recommendations for their caloric needs,
and have regular opportunities to meet with multidisciplinary team members.
A negative energy balance occurs if an individual consumes fewer calories in a day than the
overall daily caloric requirement, which varies depending on level of athletic activity, intensity
of training, and size of the athlete.7
The minimum caloric intake recommendation for females to avoid a negative energy balance is
1,800 kcal/day.7
Replenishing energy stores via a balanced diet is essential for athletic performance and
recovery.

Iron
Iron plays a fundamental role in myoglobin and hemoglobin synthesis, with iron deficiency
affecting sports performance, particularly in high-endurance athletic events. Athletes lose iron
via various pathways during training, including intravascular hemolysis, high-altitude training,

and foot-strike hemolysis.7 Female athletes have a higher risk for iron deficiency secondary to
monthly menstrual blood loss.
The bioavailability of heme iron is greater than nonheme iron sources. Heme iron is found in
animal proteins, such as seafood, chicken, and lean red meats.
Vegetarian or vegan athletes have a higher risk for iron deficiency without appropriate
supplementation because of less heme iron intake.
The daily iron intake recommendations for females vary by age7:
14 through 18 years: 15 mg/day
19 through 50 years: 18 mg/day
Iron deficiency is best identified via serum ferritin levels.7
Recognition of iron deficiency is particularly important because the repletion of iron deficiency
may require as many as 6 months of supplementation and dietary adjustments.7 Iron
supplementation in iron-deficient athletes leads to improved athletic performance by
decreasing lactate concentration, decreasing exercise heart rate, and increasing oxygen
uptake, which allows for improved work capacity during exercise.9
Vitamin D Supplementation
Vitamin D plays a key role in calcium absorption and overall bone health, specifically BMD.
Recent studies have identified the physiologic role vitamin D plays in the function and
development of the immune system, nervous system, and skeletal muscle.9,10
Vitamin D intake derives from two main sources.7
Endogenous vitamin D derives from dietary intake or supplementation.
Exogenous vitamin D derives from direct sunlight exposure and is synthesized on the skin.
Vitamin D deficiency has been linked to a higher risk for upper respiratory infections resulting
from a weakened immune response.10 This is of particular concern in female athletes because
respiratory infections are a leading medical cause of lost time from sport activities.9,10
Female athletes at high risk for vitamin D deficiency, such as individuals from northern
latitudes with decreased sunlight exposure and predominantly indoor athletic participation,
should receive 200 IU/day of vitamin D supplementation.7,10 The supplementation
requirement may increase to 400 to 800 IU/day in patients with osteoporosis or relative energy
deficiency in sport (RED-S). depending on underlying nutritional deficits.7

Females begin sweating at a higher core body temperature than males because of a higher
thermoregulatory threshold. Therefore, as core body temperature increases, even with limited
dehydration, females have more difficulty lowering core body temperature.11-13
Impaired athletic performance occurs after sweat loss that exceeds 1% to 2% of body mass
without appropriate rehydration. A comparison of pre-exercise and post-exercise weight
changes and evaluation of the urine specific gravity allows members of the sports medicine
team to assess hydration status7, 14
Water provides adequate rehydration for most training regimens; however, sports drinks or
electrolyte additives may be necessary in high-endurance athletic activities in which excessive
sweat loss requires electrolyte repletion.7
Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport
Overview
RED-S, formerly referred to as the female athlete triad, is a complex diagnosis encompassing
multiple domains. The previously described female athlete triad consisted of three domains:
low BMD, decreased energy availability that may or may not include an underlying eating
disorder, and menstrual dysfunction. RED-S expands on these core domains and emphasizes
that underlying energy deficiency affects multiple emotional, behavioral, psychosocial, and
physiologic domains.7,8,15
RED-S affects female and male athletes and has wide-reaching consequences on overall
athletic performance.15
The spectrum of involvement linked to diagnosis ranges from mild to severe involvement in
one or all domains, with as many as 15.9% of female athletes with severe involvement of all
three core domains.16
Diagnosis
Physical examination and a thorough patient history play key roles in diagnosis. Although all
female athletes are at risk, individuals who participate in activities in which a specific
sportswear weight and body image are emphasized, such as cheerleading and gymnastics,
have a higher risk.7,15
Athletes with one of the following risk factors should undergo screening: body mass index less
than 17.5 kg/m2, history of multiple stress injuries, history of eating disorder, prior low Z-score

on dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry testing, history of decreased menses within the last 12
months.17
Screening questionnaires available to sports medicine providers include the Low Energy
Availability in Females Questionnaire and the RED-S Clinical Assessment Tool, both of which
require continued validation because data show that self-reporting questionnaires alone are
not efficacious in the detection of RED-S.18-21
Providers must obtain a comprehensive menstrual history, specifically evaluating for missed or
irregular menstrual cycles in all at-risk female athletes. This history taking also should inquire
about oral contraceptive use because artificially stimulated menstrual cycles do not prevent
the deleterious effects in other domains associated with RED-S.15
Management
The treatment plan for athletes diagnosed with RED-S incorporates a multidisciplinary team
that includes a sports dietician, psychologist, primary care provider, trainer, coach, and
parents.
Management focuses on addressing the energy deficiency via dietary modifications and
supplementation with calcium and vitamin D if necessary.7,15
Cognitive behavioral therapy that focuses on the psychological consequences of RED-S also is
a proven treatment component and may help with the return of regular menstrual cycles.22,23
Athletes diagnosed with an underlying eating disorder who present with electrolyte
abnormalities, bradycardia, and/or orthostatic hypotension may require inpatient medical
admission.21,24,25 Athletes should not be cleared for return to athletic participation until the
eating disorder has been managed.15
Stress Injuries
Female athletes with energy deficiency or menstrual dysfunction have an increased risk for
stress injury, particularly during the adolescent years during which females gain a mean
additional 2% bone mass per year; they reach 90% of PBM by the end of adolescence.8
Amenorrheic adolescent females lose a mean of 2% bone mass per year, which subsequently
predisposes them to high rates of stress fractures and osteoporosis later in life.8
Females who experience more than one stress fracture should undergo dual-energy x-ray
absorptiometry to assess BMD.17

Traditional military studies suggested a threefold increase in stress fractures among female
military recruits.8 In addition, a large National Collegiate Athletic Association Division I study by
Hame et al26 on 5,900 collegiate student athletes found a twofold increase in stress fractures
among female athletes compared with male counterparts, with the highest risk being in
female track-and-field student athletes.8
Recognition and management of stress injuries require not only management of the
underlying fracture via immobilization and activity modifications but also a comprehensive
patient history.
The etiology of underlying stress factors in female athletes may be multifactorial and requires
a thorough patient history that includes evaluation of training regimen; nutrition/dietary
considerations, including vitamin D deficiency; biomechanical etiologies; menstrual history;
and sleep hygiene.17
Osteopenia and Osteoporosis
Osteopenia is defined as a Z-score of −1.0 to −2.5 standard deviations below normal age-
matched BMD.7
Osteoporosis is defined as a Z-score less than −2.5 standard deviations below mean age-
matched BMD.7
Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry is performed to measure the BMD. The T-score derives from
a comparison of a patient’s BMD to that of a healthy, young adult population.7
Management consists of pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic treatment options that include
weight-bearing exercises, smoking cessation, and vitamin D (400 to 800 IU/day) and calcium
(1,000 to 1,500 IU/day) supplementation.
Hormone replacement therapies are not recommended by the American Academy of Family
Physicians or the US Preventive Services Task Force.7,27
Degenerative Arthritis
The three greatest risk factors for osteoarthritis are genetic predisposition, obesity, and female
sex.28
Moderate exercise does not increase the risk for osteoarthritis and provides systemic benefits
to athletes.29-32

Individuals are encouraged to maintain an athletic lifestyle that emphasizes flexibility
exercises, core strengthening, low-impact strengthening routines, and cardiac exercises (water
aerobics, swimming, biking, elliptical use).33, 34 Maintenance of an exercise regimen is a key
aspect of a healthy lifestyle because decreased overall mortality has been linked to increased
physical activity.35
Conditions Unique to Female Athletes
Birth Control
The sports medicine provider has a responsibility to help the female athlete with contraceptive
options by providing accurate information about the risks and advantages of different
contraceptives that will not risk the health of the athlete or interfere with her athletic lifestyle.
Ultimately, the option of using contraception and the type of contraceptive selected are
decisions made by the individual athlete.7 Any sexually active female athlete should undergo
an annual gynecologic examination and review the best possible contraceptive options with a
physician.
Various contraceptive options are available for the female athlete, and oral contraceptive pills
(OCPs) also are prescribed for athletes who have dysmenorrhea or heavy menstrual cycles.
Female athletes who have a history of breast cancer, personal or family history of blood clots,
migraines, abnormal liver enzymes, or specific cardiac conditions should not take OCPs
because of the risk for major adverse events.7
Body image concerns and misconceptions regarding OCPs and weight gain may steer the
female athlete away from this contraceptive option;36,37 however, physicians must reiterate to
the female athlete that multiple clinical studies have determined that OCPs do not result in
weight gain or increased body fat.
Orthopaedic providers should obtain a comprehensive patient history that includes the use of
OCPs in evaluating any female athlete requiring lower extremity surgical treatment and/or
bracing that results in immobilization, such as anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction.
OCP use is a risk factor for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and may warrant concomitant DVT
prophylaxis based on individual preoperative risk stratification.38 A stratified risk-screening
tool for posttraumatic DVT in collegiate athletes is available to evaluate DVT risk.39 Currently,
no consensus statement exists with regard to the discontinuation of OCPs before surgical
management.

Exercise in Pregnancy
A 2015 consensus statement on exercise in pregnancy by the International Olympic
Committee encouraged pregnant women to “maintain an active lifestyle, i.e. mild to moderate
exercise, the limits and intensity of highly strenuous exercise on the fetus has not been
thoroughly researched.”40
Exercise in pregnancy has several advantages, which include helping manage gestational
diabetes mellitus, aiding in self-image, decreasing the risk of excessive weight gain, and
increasing core strength to decrease the risk for low back pain. Before initiating an exercise
regimen during pregnancy, the female athlete should meet with her obstetrician to review
exercise goals and develop a safe fitness regimen. Absolute contraindications to continuing an
exercise regimen include decreased fetal movement, amniotic fluid leakage, shortness of
breath before or during exercise, vaginal bleeding, chest pain, and/or dizziness.7

Psychological Factors in Female Athletics
Early participation in athletics helps female athletes develop numerous intangible attributes,
such as independence, competitiveness, social awareness, a sense of teamwork, and an ability
to handle successes/failures.41
Adolescent females involved in sports have lower rates of substance abuse, depression, and
teenage pregnancy and an increased likelihood of obtaining a high school diploma.41
Specific sports, such as cheerleading and gymnastics, place added pressures on female
athletes to strive for a specific sportswear weight and body image, putting these athletes at a
higher risk for eating disorders and nutritional deficiencies.42 The sports medicine physician
must recognize the dilemma female athletes may face regarding body image and encourage
athletes to embrace their individual body characteristics.43
Each athlete, regardless whether male or female, responds differently to various coaching and
philosophies. In general, literature supports that coaches who are successful with female
athletes emphasize the overall success of the team, and present a planned approach to
practices and competition rather than making an example of individual athletes in front of
teammates. In addition, strength is an important factor in athletic success; however, a strong
woman often is perceived as masculine and aggressive. Ultimately, this may be detrimental to
the mental health of the female athlete and should be discussed. Consider a deeper
psychological condition if the female athlete is performing at a lower level, sustaining frequent
injuries or illnesses, or losing weight. The medical provider has a responsibility to identify
these athletes and take a multidisciplinary approach, talking with coaches, parents, and other
healthcare providers because all athletes have a fear of disappointing their parents, coach, or
team. Recognizing an abnormal response to these fears should initiating intervention earlier
than later.
Young female athletes often do not find the same sense of secondary gain through sports
participation as their male counterparts, who often see sports participation as a form of
masculinity. Therefore, female athletes may struggle to express a lack of interest in continuing
to participate in sports out of fear of disappointing a parent, a coach, or the team. A somatic
complaint without structural or mechanical cause may reflect a deeper emotional issue for the

Sexual Abuse Reporting
The sports medicine provider has a responsibility to protect the safety of the female athlete in
any case of suspected abuse.
A pattern of prolonged sexual abuse of female athletes within USA Gymnastics has been well
documented in the mainstream media in recent years and serves as a grave reminder of the
consequences of a failure to speak out against behaviors that threaten female athletes’ safety.
An emphasis is placed on the coordinated effort among medical practitioners, athletic trainers,
social workers, community leaders/advocates, political figures, and athletic administrators to
create a culture of change in which female athletes can train and compete in a safe
environment free of abuse and sexual discrimination.44
Training resources for adults who are involved in youth athletics include Safe Sport45 and
United Educators.46 These resources provide training courses that aim to create a safe
environment for athletes.
Epidemiologic Differences in the Female Athlete
Overview
Female athletes sustain a higher percentage of overuse injuries than male athletes.47-49
A higher percentage of injuries in the lower extremities occurs in females compared with
males.48,50
Concussion
Concussion is a traumatic brain injury resulting in a transient disturbance of brain function.
The Concussion in Sport Group has noted several common features to clinically define
concussion.51
Female soccer and basketball players sustain considerably more concussions than males in
matched sports.52-54 The mechanism in females is more commonly a result of contact with the
playing surface, whereas the mechanism in males is the result of player-to-player contact.52

Diagnosis
If a concussion is suspected, the athlete should be removed from the playing field and
evaluated in a controlled setting, free from distraction.51
The clinician should initially rule out cervical spine injury and perform a comprehensive
neurologic examination.
Clear signs, such as loss of consciousness, balance disturbance, and tonic posturing, require
immediate removal from play.
Screening for suspected concussion should be commenced after substantial head impact or
other symptoms (eg, headache, memory disturbance).
The Sport Concussion Assessment Tool, 5th edition, is a rigorously tested and easily accessible
tool used for sideline screening.55,56
A screening tool also has been developed for children (Child Sport Concussion Assessment
Tool) and is specific to individuals aged 5 to 12 years.57
Management
The dogma of strict rest after concussion has been questioned because recent studies have
shown that early sub-symptom threshold aerobic exercise shortens recovery and possibly
reduces the incidence of delayed recovery.58
The Buffalo Concussion Treadmill Test may be used to identify heart rate at symptom
induction and then prescribe an exercise program to target 80% to 90% of the threshold heart
rate for the first 6 to 7 days. Patients should be able to progress to greater or equal to 80% of
the age predicted maximum heart rate for 20 minutes.59
Athletes then progress to more rigorous activities via a structured return-to-play protocol.
The athlete may return to sport only after completing the return-to-play protocol without
evoking a return of symptoms.
Sex-Specific Differences in Symptoms
After concussion, females demonstrate more somatic symptoms than males, including poor
memory, dizziness, fatigue, irritability in response to light and noise, headache, anxiety, and
depression.60
The symptoms in females may take longer to resolve for clearance to begin the return-to-play
protocol than those in males.61

Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome
Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) is associated with a prevalence of 20% in adolescent
athletes, with females affected at 2 to 10 times the rate of male counterparts.
The diffuse anterior knee pain in PFPS typically is insidious in onset and provoked by overuse
or underlying malalignment.
Anatomy
The patella is proximal to the trochlea if the knee is in full extension and engages the trochlea
in approximately 20° of knee flexion.
Soft-tissue constraints include the quadriceps muscle and tendon, patellar tendon, medial
patellofemoral ligament, medial patellar retinaculum, and medial patellomeniscal ligament.
Risk factors for PFPS include a large Q angle, less hip abduction strength, lower knee extension
peak torque, and less hip external rotation strength.63
Diagnosis
The presenting symptom of PFPS is anterior knee pain of an insidious onset. Mechanical
symptoms may vary.
The clinician should rule out other causes of anterior knee pain (eg, osteochondral defects,
patellofemoral instability, plica, tendinopathy; Table 4).
Risk factors for overuse, such as new exercises, increased frequency, increased intensity, or
increased duration of sports activities, also should be determined.

The cross-sectional area of the ACL is smaller in females than in males.89-93
In controlling for the size of the ligament, the female ACL has lower mechanical properties,
notably a 22.49% lower modulus of elasticity.93

proposed as a risk factor for ACL injury because an increased Q angle causes a lateral pull on

Relaxin-2 is best known for its role in ligament catabolism during pregnancy in preparation for
child delivery. Studies have shown increased binding capabilities of relaxin in the female ACL
than in the male ACL.97 Clinically, collegiate female athletes with relaxin levels higher than 6.0
pg/mL had more than a four times higher risk for ACL tear.98 Animal research has shown no
influence of estrogen or estrogen receptors on medical collateral ligament or ACL properties.99
Similarly, oral contraceptive use is not associated with ACL injury.100

ACL Reconstruction
Similar ACL reconstruction and rehabilitation strategies are used in males and females.
Zacharias et al110 reported that the risk for secondary injury (ipsilateral graft failure or
contralateral ACL injury) is 1 in 3 in skeletally immature females. This authors reported an odds
ratio of 3.0 for contralateral ACL injury; however, no differences were noted in ipsilateral graft
failure.110
Recent data from the MOON Knee Group demonstrated a 2.1 times higher risk for ACL graft
revision at a follow-up of 6 years in patients aged 14 to 22 years who were treated with the use
of a hamstring autograft versus a bone-tendon-bone autograft.111
Recent data from the STABILITY Study Group indicated decreased graft failure rates if lateral
extra-articular tenodesis as added to ACL reconstruction with the use of a hamstring autograft
(11% versus 4%).112
The return-to-play rate in Division I female soccer players is 85%;113 however, compared with
males, females had lower return-to-play rates and a higher risk of future surgical management
of the ACL.114
The perception of functional and psychological effects of ACL reconstruction during the end
phases of rehabilitation is similar in males and females.115
ACL Injury Prevention
Neuromuscular risk factors for ACL injury are thought to be correctable; therefore, several
injury preventions protocols have been developed.
Noncontact ACL injuries in females are reduced by 67% with injury prevention training
programs.116
In addition, the implementation of broad neuromuscular training programs is more cost-
effective than universal screening and neuromuscular training only for identified high-risk
athletes.117
Female athletes participating in prevention programs demonstrate increased muscle
activation, decreased landing forces, and decreased dynamic knee valgus.118,119
Continuation of these programs is paramount to success because research shows that aerobic
deconditioning occurs within 1 to 2 months postinjury and anaerobic deconditioning occurs
within 2 weeks postinjury. 120

Shoulder Instability
The shoulder does not have a deep osseous socket and, therefore, relies heavily on the
cumulative effect of dynamic stabilizers (rotator cuff and deltoid) and static stabilizers (labrum,
joint capsule, glenohumeral ligaments).
Scapular kinesis also affects shoulder stability. Motion at the scapulothoracic joint changes the
position of the glenoid in space and can alter its contribution to joint stability in various
positions.
The importance of the dynamic stabilizers and the capsular labral complex cannot be
overstated because no isometric ligaments are present in the shoulder.
Instability may be defined as traumatic or atraumatic instability, unidirectional or
multidirectional instability (MDI), or voluntary instability.
The degree of instability can be noted in several manners. Subluxation is defined as the
symptomatic translation of the glenoid on the humeral head, whereas dislocation is the
separation of the articular surfaces from one another.
A patient also may have apprehension, in which fear of subluxation or dislocation is present
on certain maneuvers or arm positioning.
A recent study from the MOON Shoulder Group found female patients to have a minimally
clinically important difference in American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons scores and higher
rates of intraoperative capsular laxity.121 The study revealed that 26.2% of female patients had
a Beighton score greater or equal to 5, compared with 3.8% in males. More females were
treated via capsular plication and fewer females underwent open Latarjet-Bristow procedures
than males. 121
Multidirectional Instability
Less than 10% of patients with shoulder instability fall into the category of MDI. MDI was
described by Neer and Foster 122 as symptomatic laxity of the shoulder in two or more
directions, with one being inferiorly.
MDI may be traumatic or caused by repetitive microtrauma as in baseball throwers, tennis

One-half of females diagnosed with MDI have generalized ligamentous laxity based on the

Femoroacetabular Impingement Syndrome
Femoroacetabular impingement syndrome is a condition of the hip joint in which abnormal
anatomy or abnormal motion causes contact between the rim of the acetabulum and the
femoral neck. This contact may cause injury to the acetabular labrum or cartilage and may
lead to arthritis.
Femoroacetabular impingement syndrome may present as cam-type, pincer-type, or
combined cam/pincer-type. In cam-type deformity, deformity is present at the head-neck
junction, whereas pincer-type deformity is defined as acetabular rim over-coverage.
Research on sex-based differences has showed greater symptomatology and functional
limitations in females than in males.130 Males also demonstrated less hip range of motion, a
greater alpha angle, and more severe intra-articular pathology.45,130
A recent study by Maerz et al45 identified a lower number of preoperative and postoperative
patient-reported outcome measures in females than in males; however, improvement from
preoperative patient-reported outcome measures to postoperative patient-reported outcome
measures was greater in females.
